title: Next Stop...Bottom

jokes.text: Artie's divorce advice: 'Always wear the same suit. That way they think it's the only one you own. They don't rape you so much on the fucking alimony.'
jokes.setup: Artie is consoling Hank about his divorce, framing it as helpful advice
jokes.punchline: The 'advice' is a cynical, specific legal deception strategy delivered with the bluntness of a man who has clearly used it himself
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Artie — worldly, profane, specific, and darkly practical. The specificity of the suit trick elevates it beyond a generic divorce joke; it sounds like hard-won experience. 'They don't rape you so much' is a brutal, funny word choice that perfectly reflects the character's unsentimental view of the world. Could only come from Artie.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: When you have meetings with her lawyer, always wear the same suit. That way they think it's the only one you own. They don't rape you so much on the fucking alimony.

jokes.text: Hank's '2:30' Chinese dentist joke: 'That is what Chinese man say when he go to dentist. He say, uh-oh. Uh-oh, my tooth hurting.'
jokes.setup: Someone tells Hank his voice-over is at 2:30
jokes.punchline: Hank launches into a rambling, racially dated, nonsensical bit about a Chinese man at the dentist — the joke isn't funny, which IS the joke about Hank
jokes.explanation: The meta-joke here is that Hank delivers a terribly outdated, misfiring bit with complete confidence — and nobody laughs. It's a character joke about how Hank thinks he's funnier than he is. The '2:30/tooth hurting' wordplay is paper-thin, which is the point. High character integration, low actual comedy craft.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: That is what Chinese man say when he go to dentist. He say, 'uh-oh. Uh-oh, my tooth hurting.'

jokes.text: Hank discovers that 'calling fans' — his big plan for total focus — means there is literally one item on his agenda besides a voice-over. The pregnant pause after 'That's all.'
jokes.setup: Hank grandly declares total focus and asks what's on the agenda
jokes.punchline: His entire day is a 2:30 voice-over. Silence follows. Hank scrambles to invent purpose by suggesting they call fans.
jokes.explanation: The comedy lives entirely in what's unsaid: Hank declared he'd channel all his energy into the show, and his entire professional day is one 2:30 voice-over. The pause at [01:05] and his scramble to generate meaning ('we have to take care of the fans') is precise Larry Sanders cringe comedy. The awkward silence IS the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Let us blow Mr. Neil Callaham's mind.

jokes.text: 'We have to really keep on top of these calls.' — Hank's upbeat recovery after the fan call disaster
jokes.setup: The fan call has apparently ended in tragedy or at minimum disaster
jokes.punchline: Hank immediately pivots to motivational manager-speak as if nothing happened
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Hank's refusal to process what just happened and his immediate pivot to hollow professional language. 'We have to really keep on top of these calls' after presumably being told the fan died is a darkly funny character beat. His quick retreat ('No, the first one kind of took the wind out of my sails') is the actual verbal punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Callaham.

jokes.text: 'No, the first one kind of took the wind out of my sails.'
jokes.setup: Darlene asks if he wants to keep going with the fan calls after the disastrous first attempt
jokes.punchline: Hank uses a sailing metaphor to describe his emotional deflation after apparently learning a fan died
jokes.explanation: The understatement here is exquisite. A fan in the hospital (presumably dead or very bad news) gets described as having 'taken the wind out of his sails.' It's Hank's self-centeredness made comically explicit — the tragedy of a stranger is reframed as an inconvenience to Hank's afternoon productivity plan. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No, the first one kind of took the wind out of my sails.

jokes.text: Larry signs off calling Sarah Jessica Parker 'Sal' — 'Do I call you Sarah or Sarah Jessica Parker? Or Sarah Jessica? Whatever you'd like. Really. Well, I'll call you Sal.'
jokes.setup: Larry is doing a post-show sign-off and awkwardly negotiates what to call his guest
jokes.punchline: After all options — Sarah, Sarah Jessica Parker, Sarah Jessica — he settles on 'Sal,' which is none of them
jokes.explanation: A compact little absurdist gem. The joke works because Larry escalates through every possible correct answer and then blows past all of them to an invented nickname. 'Sal' lands because it's completely unpredictable but feels true to Larry's weirdly casual obliviousness on camera. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Do I call you Sarah or Sarah Jessica Parker? Or Sarah Jessica?

dialogue.speaker: Sarah Jessica Parker
dialogue.line: Whatever you'd like. Really.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, I'll call you Sal.

jokes.text: Someone hands Hank pills after the taping — 'Here's some pills for later. Have a good time, all right?'
jokes.setup: Post-show pleasantries are being exchanged
jokes.punchline: Someone casually slips Hank pills as if it's a normal parting gift, normalized by the show business milieu
jokes.explanation: A quick, dark industry-insider joke about the casual drug culture of showbiz. The normalization is the joke — pills handed off with the same energy as 'drive safe.' Not exceptional, but efficiently dark.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You know, we had Patricia Arquette on the show the other night. And she died the death of a dog.

jokes.text: Hank hits on Sarah Jessica Parker by comparing her favorably to Patricia Arquette, who 'died the death of a dog,' and calling them both 'the babies' who lack savvy
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to compliment SJP as a prelude to hitting on her
jokes.punchline: His compliment is framed as 'you're better than this other woman who was terrible' — and his pickup is disastrously clumsy
jokes.explanation: The Hank seduction attempt is a showcase of spectacular social ineptitude. 'Died the death of a dog' is a vivid, insider-ish insult of a real actress. 'The kids in the business, the babies' implies he's an 'old hand,' which is itself funny given his sidekick status. Every move he makes is wrong but feels authentic to the character.

dialogue.speaker: Sarah Jessica Parker
dialogue.line: I have a boyfriend.

jokes.text: 'I have a boyfriend.' / 'Yeah. Um, do you play pool?'
jokes.setup: SJP firmly says she has a boyfriend to deflect Hank's advances
jokes.punchline: Hank ignores it completely and pivots to pool — as if 'I have a boyfriend' is a neutral statement requiring a different activity suggestion
jokes.explanation: The non-sequitur pool pivot is a perfect Hank move. He doesn't argue, doesn't acknowledge — just completely ignores the rejection and offers an alternative activity. The pause between her statement and his 'do you play pool?' is where the comedy lives. Then 'I got my own cue and balls' lands as an unintentional double entendre. Very economical cringe.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I thought we could shoot a few games. You know, I got my own cue and balls.

jokes.text: 'I got my own cue and balls.'
jokes.setup: Hank is pitching SJP on playing pool together
jokes.punchline: The phrase works as both a literal pool reference and an unintentional sexual boast — Hank seemingly unaware of the double meaning
jokes.explanation: A quick double entendre that works because Hank almost certainly doesn't realize what he said. The character obliviousness saves it from being a cheap pun. Not spectacular but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Sarah Jessica Parker
dialogue.line: Well, I have my own cue also. He's in New York, and he'll be flying in tonight.

jokes.text: SJP: 'He'll be flying in tonight. And besides, Hank, you're old enough to be my father.' / Hank: 'Ouch. How old is your father? Or was your father, in which case I'm very sorry?'
jokes.setup: SJP shuts Hank down by noting he's old enough to be her father
jokes.punchline: Hank's response is to immediately calculate whether the math actually works — and then pivot to whether her father might be dead, which makes it exponentially worse
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely excellent joke. Instead of taking the 'you're old enough to be my father' as the obvious shutdown it is, Hank treats it as a factual claim to be verified — and then covers his bases by adding the condolence option if her father is deceased. The pivot to dead-father condolence is both desperate and accidentally dark. Strong character integration, solid quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Sarah Jessica Parker
dialogue.line: Besides, Hank, you're old enough to be my father.
Ouch.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: How old is your father?

jokes.text: 'It's Matthew Broderick. I date Matthew Broderick.'
jokes.setup: Hank keeps pressing despite all rejections; SJP finally escalates her deterrent
jokes.punchline: She name-drops her real-life boyfriend (Matthew Broderick, her actual future husband) as the ultimate trump card — playing herself as a real person with a real famous boyfriend
jokes.explanation: The Larry Sanders Show's use of real celebrity guests playing themselves creates a unique meta-comedy layer. SJP deploying her real boyfriend's name as a weapon against Hank's advances is funny in the real-vs-fictional context. The show earns this kind of joke because the celebrities ARE themselves.

dialogue.speaker: Sarah Jessica Parker
dialogue.line: It's Matthew Broderick. I date Matthew Broderick.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Hey, hey, no pressure. If tomorrow's better, hey, I'm fly with that.' SJP: 'You're fly.' Hank: 'What? Is it down?'
jokes.setup: Hank tries to use the slang 'I'm fly' to sound cool and contemporary
jokes.punchline: SJP echoes it back to him; Hank immediately mishears it as a question about his zipper
jokes.explanation: A beautifully compressed joke. Hank's failed attempt at '90s slang, SJP's perfectly timed echo, and Hank's immediate zipper panic — all in three lines. The character integration is strong (Hank trying desperately to seem cool) and the wordplay pay-off is earned. Highly quotable moment.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, no pressure. If tomorrow's better, hey, I'm fly with that. You're fly.

jokes.text: Mary (on stage): 'You scared me.' Artie: 'You ain't seen nothing yet, baby.'
jokes.setup: Mary is startled by Artie appearing in the dark backstage
jokes.punchline: Artie's ominous response — 'You ain't seen nothing yet' — implies something worse is coming, delivered as if it's both a threat and a reassurance
jokes.explanation: A quick Artie moment that works on the ominous-mentor register. 'You ain't seen nothing yet' in context refers to Hank's coming spiral. Rip Torn's delivery would sell it. Efficient but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, you hate being hit on by desperate men, too?

jokes.text: Mary: 'Oh, you hate being hit on by desperate men, too?' — after Artie says he feels they have something in common
jokes.setup: Artie tells Mary he feels they have something in common
jokes.punchline: Mary immediately assumes he's hitting on her too — 'Oh, you hate being hit on by desperate men?' — reframing Artie's opener as yet another advance
jokes.explanation: Sharp comeback that also retroactively comments on the Hank scene we just saw. Mary's read on the situation is correct — she pattern-matches Artie's opener to Hank's advances, which is both funny and a good structural callback. Economy is high.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I got a bottle of champagne at home with your name on it.
And what name would that be?
Brut.

jokes.text: Hank hits on the female crew member: 'I got a bottle of champagne at home with your name on it.' / 'And what name would that be?' / 'Brut.'
jokes.setup: Hank tries a romantic champagne line on a crew member
jokes.punchline: When she asks what name, he reveals the champagne is 'Brut' — a brand name, not her name — meaning the romantic image was him literally having a bottle of Brut champagne at home
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed classic misdirection. 'A bottle of champagne with your name on it' is a standard seduction line; asking 'what name?' is a perfect straight-man response; and 'Brut' is the ideal punchline — it collapses both the romance and Hank's pretension simultaneously. He had a bottle of Brut at home. Not a romantic gesture. Just Brut. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, I like them small and compact.

dialogue.speaker: Stage Manager
dialogue.line: Then why don't you go fuck a Toyota?

jokes.text: Crew member: 'Then why don't you go fuck a toyota?'
jokes.setup: Hank says 'I like them small and compact' — ostensibly referring to the woman's figure
jokes.punchline: She responds by suggesting he should fuck a Toyota — weaponizing his own phrasing against him
jokes.explanation: A viciously funny comeback that works on pure logical extension — if he likes small and compact, she provides the ultimate small-compact option. The Toyota specificity is perfect: not just 'a car,' but a Toyota. Blunt, fast, devastating. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Wow, and a sense of humor.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Wow, and a sense of humor.' — after being told to go fuck a Toyota
jokes.setup: He was just brutally rejected and insulted
jokes.punchline: Hank reframes the devastating insult as an attractive quality — 'and a sense of humor!' — as if the Toyota line proved she'd be great company
jokes.explanation: This is pure Hank character comedy. The inability to process rejection — turning an insult into a compliment — is a perfect expression of his delusion. The economy is near-perfect. It also makes the Toyota joke even funnier retroactively.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Wow, and a sense of humor. No one loves me. No one really cares.

jokes.text: Hank: 'No one loves me. No one really cares.' / Artie: 'I do.' — Hank's self-pitying collapse
jokes.setup: Hank collapses into self-pity after being rejected by every woman backstage
jokes.punchline: Artie's simple 'I do' — unironic, warm, matter-of-fact — functions as both genuine and darkly comic given the context
jokes.explanation: The brevity of 'I do' is perfect. It's played straight, which makes it both funny and surprisingly touching — a rare moment of genuine warmth in a cynical show, made comedic by its contrast with everything that preceded it.

dialogue.line: Tight little body. Your breasts.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.line: Hank! Come on.

jokes.text: Artie's confessional about keeping 'professional distance': 'admiring your hair... tight little body... your breasts.' Escalating, then caught.
jokes.setup: Artie tells Darlene he keeps professional distance while admiring her qualities
jokes.punchline: Each pause reveals he's been cataloguing increasingly intimate physical attributes — 'your hair... tight little body... your breasts' — before being called out
jokes.explanation: The structural escalation — hair (professional) → body (borderline) → breasts (explicit) — is well-paced and earns its cringe. Each beat lands a little harder. Artie is established as a relatively dignified character, so this undermines him in a funny way. The [06:27] and [06:32] timestamps capture the pauses that make the escalation work.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: After my first wife gave me the gate, I went on a binge of sex, drugs, and 180-proof Everclear that lasted for three years.

jokes.text: Artie explains divorce stages to Darlene: 'Shock, denial, fear, booze, boners, acceptance.'
jokes.setup: Artie describes the six stages of healing after a divorce with clinical authority
jokes.punchline: The list — 'shock, denial, fear, booze, boners, acceptance' — starts like Kübler-Ross grief stages and then goes deeply off the rails
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode and one of the best Larry Sanders Show jokes as a unit. The setup is perfect: Artie invokes real psychological language ('six stages of healing') to give authority to his framework. The list begins plausibly (shock, denial, fear) — recognizable echoes of Kübler-Ross — then pivots with 'booze' (funny but still credible for Artie) and then hits 'boners' before landing on 'acceptance.' The placement of 'boners' just before the legitimate final stage ('acceptance') is structurally perfect. Only Artie can deliver this. Incredibly quotable. High rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: After my fourth divorce, I was able to squeeze the same amount of debauchery into a long weekend.

jokes.text: Artie's divorce binge story: 'After my first wife gave me the gate, I went on a binge of sex, drugs, and 180-proof Everclear that lasted three years. After my fourth divorce, I was able to squeeze the same amount of debauchery into a long weekend. But I have a scar from that one.'
jokes.setup: Artie is counseling Darlene about Hank's behavior, speaking from personal experience
jokes.punchline: The three-year binge compresses to a long weekend by divorce #4, demonstrating efficient corruption — but then the 'I have a scar from that one' adds a dark kicker
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. The concept of compressing three years of debauchery into a long weekend by divorce #4 is both funny and character-revealing — Artie as a man who has refined dissolution into an art form. '180-proof Everclear' is a specific, vivid detail. And 'I have a scar from that one' is a perfect dark button that implies something catastrophic without specifying. Pure Artie. Could only be this character.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Shock, denial, fear, booze, boners, acceptance.

jokes.text: Artie's six stages listed again as a callback/confirmation: 'Shock, denial, fear, booze, boners, acceptance' — Darlene's 'I've just never seen him as a sex-and-drugs kind of guy' sets it up
jokes.setup: Darlene is worried about Hank; Artie references his six stages framework
jokes.punchline: The stages are laid out explicitly, confirming the framework first mentioned — now with Darlene's naïve reaction as counterpoint
jokes.explanation: The explicit listing of the stages is slightly less impactful than the first delivery but still earns a laugh as it's delivered in full. Darlene's skepticism about Hank as a 'sex-and-drugs kind of guy' is a nice straight-man beat.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, how much just to jack me off?

dialogue.speaker: Prostitute
dialogue.line: 150 cash up front.

jokes.text: Cut to Hank in a hotel room with a prostitute — 'Well, how much just to jack me off?' / '150 cash up front.' / 'What do you mean, up front?'
jokes.setup: Artie has described Hank being in a 'spiritual tailspin' — cut immediately to Hank with a prostitute
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition of 'I'm worried about him, he'll find someone to talk to' cutting directly to Hank negotiating sexual services is a structural joke
jokes.explanation: The scene cut itself is a structural joke — Artie's 'maybe a trusted member of the clergy' line is immediately answered by Hank negotiating with a prostitute. The cut earns its laugh from pure comic juxtaposition. The negotiation itself is cringe-funny, with Hank pushing back on the 'up front' policy with genuine consternation.

dialogue.speaker: Prostitute
dialogue.line: You know, when you go to a gas station, they ask you to pay first, so it's a precedent, you know.

jokes.text: Hank pushes back on the 'up front' payment policy: 'That's a new policy, isn't it? Easier that way. You know, when you go to a gas station, they ask you to pay first, so it's a precedent, you know.'
jokes.setup: The prostitute explains the new cash-up-front policy
jokes.punchline: She justifies it with the gas station analogy — a weirdly rational business explanation in an irrational context — and Hank accepts 'it's a precedent' as reasonable
jokes.explanation: The gas station/prostitution business analogy is absurdly funny in context. The prostitute explaining her payment policy with consumer-economy logic normalizes the transaction in a darkly comic way. Hank accepting 'it's a precedent' is both in-character and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Prostitute
dialogue.line: When you go to a gas station, they ask you to pay first, so it's a precedent, you know.

jokes.text: Hank's emotional disclosure to the prostitute: 'I think I should tell you, I just have a real need to... feel loved tonight.' / Prostitute: 'Yeah, me, too.'
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to establish emotional intimacy with the sex worker
jokes.punchline: Her 'Yeah, me, too' is delivered as deadpan professional agreement — whether genuine or not is irrelevant; the symmetry is funny
jokes.explanation: The prostitute's deadpan mirroring of Hank's emotional disclosure works because it's ambiguous — is she playing along professionally, or does she actually mean it? Either reading is funny in context. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Prostitute
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey. No. No kissing. I don't work that way.

jokes.text: 'No kissing. I don't work that way.' — the prostitute refusing to kiss Hank
jokes.setup: Hank was establishing how much he needs intimacy and connection
jokes.punchline: The prostitute, who will do other things, draws the line specifically at kissing — a Pretty Woman-style rule that undercuts Hank's emotional framing
jokes.explanation: A fairly standard 'no kissing' prostitute trope, but earns points for being deployed in a context where Hank has just been talking about needing to feel loved. The irony is the comedy. Not original, but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Prostitute
dialogue.line: Used to make cat noises when I blew him. Jeez. You kind of look like him.

jokes.text: Hank explaining he's trying to 'replace some of the intimacy I had with her with you' — the long pause after
jokes.setup: Hank tries to explain his emotional need for the transaction
jokes.punchline: The [09:14] beat — the pause after his explanation — is the punchline. Nothing she can say makes this better.
jokes.explanation: The pause is doing the work here. Hank has articulated something so nakedly sad that only silence can follow. In a show without a laugh track, this kind of beat lands as both uncomfortable and darkly funny.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Rrrr. Mmm. Woof! I'm all right. Aiiee. Arf, arf.

jokes.text: 'You have no idea who I am, do you?' / 'Thought for a minute I had an idea.'
jokes.setup: Hank is in his existential crisis mode; asks the prostitute if she knows who he is
jokes.punchline: Her 'thought for a minute I had an idea' implies she started to recognize him and then lost it — perfectly deflating
jokes.explanation: Perfect for Hank's arc this episode — the show's central theme (his invisibility when not next to Larry) is literalized in his inability to be recognized even by a prostitute who has been with him. 'Thought for a minute I had an idea' is a precisely deflating line.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hank's not doing the show? How will we survive? Will there be a tomorrow? God in heaven, save us!

jokes.text: 'And don't call me mister, all right?'
jokes.setup: Hank has paid for sex and is explaining his emotional needs to the prostitute
jokes.punchline: His objection to 'mister' — wanting something more familiar — in this context is the distilled essence of his loneliness and delusion
jokes.explanation: Three words that reveal an entire emotional state. Hank has just handed a stranger $150 and is now asking for the illusion of familiarity. The economy is exceptional — this tiny objection contains Hank's entire pathology.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I'm in show business, so I'm a little bit of a whore, too.

jokes.text: The prostitute's story about a guy from Hermosa Beach who made 'cat noises' while she 'blew him' — 'You kind of look like him.'
jokes.setup: The prostitute is making conversation with Hank
jokes.punchline: Her anecdote about the cat-noise man ends with 'You kind of look like him' — which is both an insult and an unsettling recognition
jokes.explanation: The cat-noise detail is a genuinely original, vivid comedy choice. The anecdote pivots from describing a bizarre stranger to implicating Hank — which deepens his humiliation. Hank's 'Some people are really fucked up' as a response to a story that may be about him is a nice double-read.

dialogue.speaker: Prostitute
dialogue.line: You calling me a whore?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I'm not calling you a whore. No, no. I'm just saying that, you know, you're different from the other wh... from the other girls.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Some people are really fucked up.' — said in response to the cat-noise prostitute story that may be about him
jokes.setup: The prostitute tells an anecdote that appears to be about Hank
jokes.punchline: Hank's oblivious judgment of 'some people' when he is in a hotel room with a prostitute during a breakdown is ironic self-commentary
jokes.explanation: The irony is thick: Hank judging the behavior of others from his current position. The lack of self-awareness is the comedy. Five words doing a lot of work.

dialogue.speaker: Prostitute
dialogue.line: One time I did this guy named... uh, what's his name? Andy Richter.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Get out.

jokes.text: The prostitute makes animal sounds during sex — 'Rrrr... Woof! Arf, arf.' — apparently unsolicited or professional habit
jokes.setup: The callback from the cat-noise story — she described a client who made cat noises; she now makes animal sounds herself
jokes.punchline: The sounds escalate from a cat-ish growl to dog barks — 'Woof! Arf, arf.' — suggesting either she's also into it or mimicking the client she described
jokes.explanation: The callback to the cat-noise story is structurally elegant — she described it as something a client did, and now she's doing it. Whether this is performance, habit, or identification with the previous client is left ambiguous, which is funnier than any explanation would be. The escalation from 'Rrrr' to 'Woof! Arf arf' is absurdist and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Prostitute
dialogue.line: God, you sidekicks are all alike.

jokes.text: Artie tells Larry Hank has 'food poisoning' and to 'take care of both ends' — a crude euphemism covering for Hank's actual situation
jokes.setup: Artie is on the phone covering for Hank's absence with a fiction
jokes.punchline: The 'take care of both ends' advice, meant innocuously about food poisoning, works as an inadvertent description of what Hank is actually doing
jokes.explanation: The irony of 'take care of both ends' while Hank is with a prostitute is a quiet dirty joke that the show leaves implicit. Only works on rewatch or for audiences tracking both storylines simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Network Executive
dialogue.line: A friend of mine said that he saw Mr. Kingsley sitting in a hotel bar with a prostitute.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Your friend is mistaken.

jokes.text: Larry (sarcastically panicking): 'Hank's not doing the show? How will we survive? Will there be a tomorrow? God in heaven, save us!'
jokes.setup: Artie reports that Hank isn't coming in and asks Larry to cover
jokes.punchline: Larry's escalating theatrical despair about Hank's absence — 'God in heaven, save us!' — reveals his true feelings about Hank's replacability
jokes.explanation: Larry's sarcasm is richly in character — he's the star and Hank is replaceable, but the show makes it explicit through Larry's mock panic. 'God in heaven, save us!' is a beautifully overwrought button. This is classic Larry Sanders: darkness behind the professionalism.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: He sees a bald man with a hooker. Automatically, it's Hank Kingsley. I wasn't aware Carl Reiner's out of town.

jokes.text: The therapist/expert explains that post-divorce people get 'sexually promiscuous' — immediately cuts back to Hank with his prostitute
jokes.setup: Artie and Darlene (or a professional) are discussing post-divorce psychology in clinical terms
jokes.punchline: The clinical explanation of sexual promiscuity is intercut with or immediately followed by Hank's hotel-room situation
jokes.explanation: The structural juxtaposition of the clinical explanation and Hank's situation is a classic sitcom device, but Larry Sanders uses it with enough specificity that it feels fresh. The longer clinical speech makes the irony more sustained.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You only care about me because you're my agent. I pay you 10% to care about me.

dialogue.speaker: Sid
dialogue.line: 7½%, you cheap bastard.

jokes.text: Hank to the prostitute: 'You know, you and I should go out on a date sometime. Not like this. A real date. Just have fun.'
jokes.setup: Hank is in the middle of paying for sex
jokes.punchline: He pivots to suggesting they go on a 'real date' — distinguishing it from the current transaction as if this could become something
jokes.explanation: The romantic pivot while paying for sex is perfectly Hank — unable to process transactions as transactions, always seeking something more, which of course drives his divorce. 'Not like this. A real date.' is painfully revealing character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Sid
dialogue.line: You've been married to the same lady for 56 years. I'm thinking of getting out.

jokes.text: Prostitute: 'I don't date the guys I do.' / Hank: 'Well, now listen. We have a lot in common. I'm in show business, so I'm a little bit of a whore, too.'
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to establish common ground with the prostitute after she refuses to date clients
jokes.punchline: He lands on 'I'm in show business, so I'm a little bit of a whore, too' — the show business/prostitution equivalence delivered as flattery
jokes.explanation: A classically Larry Sanders observation — the show is always about the performative, transactional nature of show business. Hank comparing himself to a prostitute as a point of CONNECTION is both funny and accidentally profound. 'I'm a little bit of a whore, too' is the kind of self-aware confession that Hank delivers without full self-awareness. Strong economy, high quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Helen
dialogue.line: I did him once. In 1956. It was only the one time. Now we're dear, dear friends.

jokes.text: Hank: 'I'm not calling you a whore. No, no. I'm just saying that, you know, you're different from the other wh... from the other girls.'
jokes.setup: The prostitute reacts to being called a whore; Hank immediately backpedals
jokes.punchline: His correction fails mid-word — 'other wh...' — before he catches himself, but the damage is done
jokes.explanation: The mid-word self-correction is a comedy writing technique that requires precise execution — 'other wh...' The slippage reveals exactly what he was about to say. The recovery is even worse: 'from the other girls.' Beautifully structured verbal fumble. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Darlene, he's hit bottom and broke through to another bottom I know nothing about.

jokes.text: Prostitute: 'You're not the first sidekick I've been with. One time I did this guy named... Andy Richter. Get out.' / Hank: 'Go on.' / Prostitute: 'But you paid for the whole night.'
jokes.setup: Hank has been talking about being a sidekick; the prostitute reveals she has sidekick experience
jokes.punchline: Andy Richter — Conan's real sidekick — name-dropped as a previous client; Hank demands she leave but is reminded he paid for the whole night
jokes.explanation: A standout industry-insider joke. Andy Richter is the real-world sidekick equivalent of Hank — which makes him the perfect name to deploy here. Hank's ego is so wounded by the comparison that he tries to throw her out despite having paid for the night. The pivot 'But you paid for the whole night' is the practical anchor that makes the absurdist scenario concrete. The 'sidekick solidarity' implication is darkly funny. High quotability, strong rewatch.

dialogue.speaker: Raoul
dialogue.line: Great show last night. You were really funny, as always. Hold on. What's your name? Raoul.

jokes.text: Prostitute: 'Sheesh. God, you sidekicks are all alike.' / Hank: 'I heard that.'
jokes.setup: The prostitute comments on sidekick behavior as she's being kicked out
jokes.punchline: 'You sidekicks are all alike' delivered as if she's categorizing a demographic; Hank's indignant 'I heard that' from another room
jokes.explanation: The prostitute having enough sidekick experience to have formed a generalization is absurdly funny. 'You sidekicks are all alike' works because it treats Hank's professional category as a personality type she's professionally familiar with. 'I heard that' as offscreen indignation is the perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: And that is the effect, apparently, that I'm having on the American fucking viewing public!

jokes.text: Artie at the hotel bar: meets Paul Wallum from the network, immediately recalls his drunk Christmas party details — 'Wife named Karen. Children... Michael, Lucy. Dog... Ginger.'
jokes.setup: Paul Wallum reintroduces himself to Artie from the Christmas party
jokes.punchline: Artie immediately recalls absurdly specific details — wife, children, dog — apparently retained despite being hammered; Wallum is impressed; Artie explains he was 'Hammered'
jokes.explanation: Artie's drunk-but-observant party behavior is a nice character detail. The punchline — 'Hammered. That would pretty well cover it' — is the kind of honest understatement Rip Torn would sell perfectly. The implication that he memorizes people's family details while drunk is both funny and slightly unsettling.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Raul Julia was here?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Raoul the waiter.

jokes.text: Artie's indignant defense of Hank: 'Are you trying to imply that I wouldn't know of the whereabouts of my sidekick? Are you trying to suggest that I am so incompetent that I wouldn't know if Hank Kingsley was avoiding work so he could fuck a whore?'
jokes.setup: Wallum suggests Hank was seen with a prostitute; Artie denies all knowledge
jokes.punchline: Artie's denial escalates into an outraged rhetorical question that is technically a complete description of exactly what Hank is doing — he's denying it by accidentally stating it precisely
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly structured denial joke. Artie's strategy is bluster, and his bluster contains a perfectly accurate description of Hank's actual situation: 'avoiding work so he could fuck a whore.' The comedy is that his outrage proves he knows exactly what's happening. The rhetorical escalation ('Are you trying to imply... are you trying to SUGGEST') is textbook Artie. Could only be this character in this situation.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: This is a Beretta 9mm Centurion. You just pick that baby up. It'll do the job for you.

jokes.text: Artie: 'He sees a bald man with a hooker. Automatically, it's Hank Kingsley. I wasn't aware Carl Reiner's out of town.'
jokes.setup: Artie is dismissing the eyewitness by pointing out a bald man with a hooker doesn't have to be Hank
jokes.punchline: The alternative he offers is Carl Reiner — implying Carl Reiner routinely frequents prostitutes, which is both absurd and specific
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The joke requires: (1) knowing Carl Reiner is bald, (2) understanding that Artie is deflecting by proposing an alternative bald-man suspect, (3) appreciating that Carl Reiner is simultaneously an absurd and perfect choice — respectable enough to be funny, Jewish-Hollywood-adjacent enough to fit the show's milieu. 'I wasn't aware Carl Reiner's out of town' implies Carl Reiner is usually the one you'd expect to see with a hooker. Rip Torn's delivery would be immaculate. High originality, perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Listen, I'm gonna give housekeeping 20 bucks. I mean, you won't feel a fucking thing, but they're the ones who are gonna have to suffer.

jokes.text: Hank on the phone with his agent Sid: 'I pay you 10% to care about me.' / Sid: '7½%, you cheap bastard.'
jokes.setup: Hank tells Sid he only cares because he's his agent — 'I pay you 10% to care about me'
jokes.punchline: Sid corrects the commission rate — 7½% — as his first priority, functionally proving Hank's point about the transactional nature of their relationship
jokes.explanation: A perfect agent joke. Hank says he pays for care; Sid immediately corrects the rate from 10% to 7½% — which is EXACTLY what a transactional agent would prioritize, thus confirming Hank's cynical point while also undermining it (Sid knows the exact number; he does track this). Economy is near-perfect. 'You cheap bastard' as the button is exactly right.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No one cares because I'm the boss. The boss has no problems. Sometimes, I swear to God, I feel like I should just end it all.

jokes.text: Sid's advice: 'Hank, don't be such a putz with the hookers. What you need is a special woman. I mean a hooker. Somebody who's discrete, can be trusted. Somebody who doesn't look like a hooker. That would be very special, indeed.'
jokes.setup: Sid tells Hank he needs a 'special woman' — which sounds like romantic advice
jokes.punchline: The clarification is immediate: not a wife, 'I mean a hooker' — but one who is discreet and 'doesn't look like a hooker,' which Sid frames as 'very special indeed'
jokes.explanation: The misdirection pivot ('Not a wife. I mean a hooker.') works because Sid delivers it as if this is sound, sensible advice — and it is, in the logic of this world. 'That would be very special, indeed' is a perfect deadpan button. This is the Hollywood old-guard cynicism that defines the show.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You can always blow your head off. Safety's off. Ready to go. The divorce gun.

jokes.text: Artie's confessional: 'Yeah, I've known Sid for close to 40 years now. I kid you not. Sid is a good man. I did him once. In 1956. It was only the one time. Now we're dear, dear friends.'
jokes.setup: Artie gives a talking-head testimonial about his relationship with Sid
jokes.punchline: 'I did him once. In 1956. It was only the one time. Now we're dear, dear friends.' — a matter-of-fact, historically situated sexual confession delivered as if describing a lunch
jokes.explanation: The best single joke in the episode. The setup is a genuine 40-year-friendship testimonial; the pivot — 'I did him once' — arrives with no warning and is delivered with perfect deadpan normality. '1956' adds absurd historical specificity. 'It was only the one time' manages the implication with a delicate lie. 'Now we're dear, dear friends' reframes a sexual encounter as the foundation of a lifelong friendship. The structure is immaculate: setup, confession, qualification, closure. Artie's voice delivering this is the cherry on top. This is the kind of joke that defines a show.

dialogue.line: How close did Hank come to shooting himself?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, that fucking baby. He started crying the second I pulled it out.

jokes.text: The high-end prostitute Sid arranged: 'Hmm. You were amazing last night. And I can honestly say that you are the nicest young man that Sid ever introduced me to.'
jokes.setup: Artie has told us Sid knows a 'special' woman; we now see this woman with Hank
jokes.punchline: She implies Sid routinely introduces her to clients — 'the nicest young man Sid ever introduced me to' — confirming this is a regular Sid service and simultaneously complimenting Hank in a very relative way
jokes.explanation: A payoff joke for Sid's 'special hooker' advice. The reveal that Sid has a stable of introductions is darkly funny, and 'nicest young man Sid ever introduced me to' damns Sid's other referrals. Good structural payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Gosh, this brings back memories.

jokes.text: 'Gonna share that doobie, sweetheart?' — Artie in the hotel room with Sid's prostitute and Hank, casually asking to share a joint
jokes.setup: Artie has come to the hotel to check on Hank; the scene has resolved into relative calm
jokes.punchline: Artie asks to share a joint as if this is a completely normal way to conclude a crisis intervention
jokes.explanation: Perfect Artie moment. After navigating a potential suicide crisis, getting a prostitute involved, confronting the network man — he asks to share a joint with perfect casualness. Character integration is excellent. Economy is excellent. The normalization of the chaos is the joke.

jokes.text: Artie on the phone: 'Is he OK?' / Artie: 'Darlene, he's hit bottom and broke through to another bottom I know nothing about.'
jokes.setup: Darlene asks if Hank is okay
jokes.punchline: 'He's hit bottom and broke through to another bottom I know nothing about' — a metaphor of such concentrated despair delivered with complete equanimity
jokes.explanation: One of the great lines of the series. 'Hit bottom and broke through to another bottom I know nothing about' is structurally elegant: it extends the 'rock bottom' metaphor logically into absurdism — there are multiple bottoms, and Hank has discovered a sub-basement of degradation. Artie's calm delivery ('Got to roll') is the perfect non-reaction to this extraordinary statement. Extraordinarily quotable, strong rewatch value.

jokes.text: Raoul the bellhop tells Hank he was 'really funny as always' on last night's show — Hank wasn't on the show.
jokes.setup: Raoul compliments Hank on being funny on last night's show
jokes.punchline: Hank wasn't on the show — and he's been absent all week
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's thematic core turned into a joke: Hank's absence is so unremarkable that a regular viewer couldn't tell he wasn't there. The fan-call joke established that Hank's connection to his audience is tenuous; this confirms it from the opposite direction — an audience member who watched and couldn't notice the absence. Devastating for Hank, funny for the audience.

jokes.text: Hank makes Raoul watch a recording of the show on TV to prove he isn't on it — pointing at the screen: 'I'm not there. Why is that do you suppose?'
jokes.setup: Hank wants Raoul to understand the magnitude of his invisibility
jokes.punchline: He makes a hotel bellhop watch TV to verify his own absence — the visual of Hank pointing at a screen where he doesn't appear
jokes.explanation: A rich visual-cringe moment. Hank's desperation to have his absence acknowledged — forcing a bellhop to watch TV — is pathetically funny. 'Why is that do you suppose?' asked of a confused hotel worker is a perfectly absurd escalation of the existential crisis. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Hank throws Raoul out: 'You get out. And you come back in here, I'll kill you, you little prick.' / Then: 'Raoul. You little... prick.'
jokes.setup: Hank has had his breakdown and is expelling the witness
jokes.punchline: The repeated 'prick' — once in fury, then again in a lower register after the door closes — suggests he's rehearsing the insult for his own comfort
jokes.explanation: The repeated 'prick' in diminuendo — screamed and then murmured — captures Hank's deflation nicely. The second utterance is the comedy; the first is just anger. Character-specific but not exceptional writing.

jokes.text: Artie reunites with Helen at the hotel — she's a sex worker he apparently knew years ago. 'How's Stan and the kids? Beautiful Joanne is in New York doing God knows what. Stan had a bypass operation. That's why I'm back on my back.'
jokes.setup: Artie warmly greets Helen as an old acquaintance catching up on life updates
jokes.punchline: 'That's why I'm back on my back' — Helen explains her return to sex work as a result of Stan's medical bills, delivered as a casual update in an otherwise warm reunion
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of a warm family update — kids, IBM job, bypass surgery — with 'that's why I'm back on my back' is perfectly executed dark comedy. The phrase 'back on my back' is simultaneously crude and euphemistic. The warm reunion context makes it even funnier: this is as natural a conversation as any old friends would have. Strong economy and character integration (only in the Larry Sanders world).

jokes.text: Hank's existential breakdown: 'Artie, what am I doing here? What did I do with my life? Who am I?' / Artie: 'You're Hank Kingsley. You're the best goddamn sidekick in the business. And that includes the great Al Gore. Don't you fucking forget that.'
jokes.setup: Hank spirals into genuine existential crisis
jokes.punchline: Artie's pep talk culminates in 'the great Al Gore' — comparing Hank favorably to the Vice President as a sidekick to Clinton
jokes.explanation: A brilliant topical joke with lasting resonance. Artie's attempt at a pep talk — 'the best goddamn sidekick in the business, and that includes the great Al Gore' — reframes the Vice President as a sidekick, which is both politically subversive and perfectly logical in the show's framework (politicians as performers, VPs as sidekicks). The specificity of 'the great Al Gore' makes it extraordinary. Could only work in this show, with this character, at this political moment. High quotability.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Raul Julia was here?' / Hank: 'Raoul the waiter.' / Artie: 'Oh, man, you're going paranoid. Listen to the way you talk.'
jokes.setup: Hank mentions 'Raoul' in the context of his breakdown about being unrecognized
jokes.punchline: Artie mishears it as 'Raul Julia' — the famous actor — and then diagnoses Hank's 'paranoia' as the problem when Hank clarifies it was just a waiter
jokes.explanation: A nimble name-confusion joke. 'Raul Julia was here?' treats the situation as a celebrity sighting rather than a bellhop anecdote. The pivot to accusing Hank of paranoia ('listen to the way you talk') is Artie being Artie — deflecting and slightly gaslighting simultaneously. Clean, quick, funny.

jokes.text: Artie produces a loaded gun: 'Whoa, Jesus Christ, is that thing loaded?' / 'You bet it's loaded. This is a Beretta 9mm centurion. You just pick that baby up. It'll do the job for you. It'll be painless, quick. Just put it in your hand, pull the trigger.'
jokes.setup: Hank says he wants to 'end it all'; Artie takes him seriously — or appears to
jokes.punchline: Artie pulls out a real, loaded gun and encourages Hank to use it — describing its specs and efficiency as if recommending a product
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in dark comedy tension. The shock of Artie producing a real gun when someone has just said they want to end it all is audacious. His product-review description of the Beretta ('It'll do the job for you. Painless, quick.') is both horrifying and hilarious. The joke is that Artie's crisis-intervention technique is to provide the means — and it works, because the gun shocks Hank out of his spiral. The housekeeping tipping detail ('I'm gonna give housekeeping 20 bucks') is the perfect specificity that makes it land.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Listen, I'm gonna give housekeeping 20 bucks. I mean, you won't feel a fucking thing, but they're the ones who are gonna have to suffer. They're gonna have to clean up this mess, so just go on, hurry up! Pick it up! Put your hand on it! Come on! Don't drag this thing out!'
jokes.setup: Artie is 'encouraging' Hank to shoot himself with the loaded gun
jokes.punchline: His concern for the housekeeping staff — tipping them $20 to clean up the mess — is a pitch-black comedy of practical concern amid the absurd
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's great moments. Artie's crisis-intervention-by-enablement escalates into him shouting 'Come on! Don't drag this thing out!' as if Hank is procrastinating on a chore. The housekeeping tip ($20 for a suicide cleanup) is the most Artie-specific detail imaginable — practical, cheap, dark. The escalating urgency ('Pick it up! Put your hand on it! Come on!') is masterfully written. This is HBO comedy at its most distinctive.

jokes.text: Artie's actual intervention: 'Aw, sweetheart. Hey, you don't wanna kill yourself. If you did, you would've done it before now.'
jokes.setup: The gun approach has worked — Hank is crying rather than shooting
jokes.punchline: 'If you did, you would've done it before now' — Artie's comforting logic for why Hank won't kill himself is that he hasn't already
jokes.explanation: A perfect line. 'If you did, you would've done it before now' is simultaneously terrible and brilliant suicide-prevention logic — it's tautological, slightly callous, and yet oddly comforting. It reframes suicidal ideation as evidence of its own falsity. Only Artie would think to say this, and only Rip Torn could deliver it with the required deadpan warmth. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: Artie's prediction: 'In a couple of years, you'll be married again, maybe to a strawberry blonde this time. And in a year, you'll get divorced again, and you'll wind up in this very hotel, maybe with Helen.'
jokes.setup: Artie is convincing Hank to come back to work and stop wallowing
jokes.punchline: His vision of Hank's positive future is: another marriage, another divorce, same hotel, possibly the same prostitute. 'C'est la vie.'
jokes.explanation: Artie's hopeful future for Hank — another divorce, same hotel, maybe Helen — is darkly hilarious because it treats the cycle of destructive behavior as the natural order of things. 'C'est la vie' as the button is perfect. The callback to Helen specifically is structurally satisfying.

jokes.text: Hank: 'That's a real gun?' / Artie: 'What do you think these fucking notches are?' / Hank: 'Oh... gimme the gun, just for a second. I just wanna scare this little shit.'
jokes.setup: Hank is recovering; he notices the gun has notches
jokes.punchline: Artie confirms it's real and has been used ('what do you think these fucking notches are?'); Hank, just talked down from suicide, immediately wants to use it to threaten someone
jokes.explanation: A perfect character beat. Hank is just talked down from a suicide attempt — and his immediate instinct is to redirect the weapon outward ('just wanna scare this little shit'). The notches on a real gun as casual Artie inventory is brilliant. The snap from suicidal to aggressive is darkly funny and completely true to Hank's narcissism.

jokes.text: Artie presents the gun to Larry: 'You can always blow your head off. Safety's off. Ready to go. The divorce gun. Gosh, this brings back memories.'
jokes.setup: Larry is venting about wanting to end it all; Artie produces the gun again
jokes.punchline: 'The divorce gun' — the gun has a name, implying it's been used therapeutically before. 'Gosh, this brings back memories' confirms a history of deployment.
jokes.explanation: The callback and escalation together make this one of the episode's finest moments. The gun has now earned a title — 'the divorce gun' — implying Artie deploys it regularly as a crisis management tool. 'Gosh, this brings back memories' is delivered with the nostalgia of a beloved ritual object. The gun being named is an absurdist detail of the highest order. Only possible in this show, with this character. Among the most quotable lines in the episode.

jokes.text: Final talking head — someone asks how close Hank came to shooting himself. Artie: 'Oh, that fucking baby. He started crying the second I pulled it out.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks Artie to assess the genuine danger of the situation
jokes.punchline: 'That fucking baby. He started crying the second I pulled it out.' — Artie reveals the gun tactic was never in doubt and Hank's response was immediate tears
jokes.explanation: The perfect button for the episode. Artie's dismissive 'that fucking baby' retroactively reveals his gun tactic was calculated shock therapy — he always knew Hank wouldn't go through with it, and the crying confirmed it instantly. 'He started crying the second I pulled it out' is funny on its own and devastating as an epilogue. The whole dark gun sequence is recontextualized as confident Artie improvisation. Economy and character integration are perfect. One of the great closing talking-head lines.

tmdb_overview: A depressed and unhappy Hank hits on all the female guests before retreating to a hotel room for a boozy marathon with a series of prostitutes.
